title: Rise and fall of heavy cavalry
blurb: From a tame horse pulling a chariot to the salaried musketeer that retired the knight — 4000 years of military dominance, none of it planned.

steps.edge_note: Domestication turned occasional drags into daily logistics; sledges exhausted people and animals until rolling bearings amortized the load.

The cart already posed the question “what pulls this?” Horses were drafted into that existing vehicle economy—chariot warfare is cart-tech meeting a faster animal, not the invention of mounted combat.
Charioteers could brace reins on the yoke; a solo rider has no third hand, so steering has to migrate to the mouth or control falls apart at speed.
Mouth control answers direction; it does not absorb fighting shocks or spare the spine—without a weight spreader the mount fails before the rider does.
A seat alone leaves the torso swimming sideways; hanging footholds buy the first real lateral purchase for archery—at the price of splintering under a melee hit.
The geometry was already right; wood was the weak link. Metallurgy is what lets the same loop survive the impact that proved leather and timber could not.
This is not a detour: knight-weight mounts come from draft breeding, and draft breeding followed plow teams that could work northern clay—agrarian horsepower funds cavalry horsepower.
Stirrups fix side-to-side; a couched lance still punches you out the back—so the next failure mode is longitudinal recoil, not leverage.
Biomechanics solved, the bottleneck shifts to infrastructure: stone roads and campaigns grind hooves faster than unshod animals can sustain repeated charges.
Shod, braced, cantled riders can finally spend the horse’s momentum budget on one pointed impulse instead of husbanding the animal’s feet.
Shock cavalry is a calorie business; the collar is the farm-side multiplier that turns northern clay into surplus grain—and surplus grain into estates that can feed destriers.
The same centuries that perfected heavy cavalry also produced a weapon that ignores the contact zone entirely: plate and horse do not argue with yardage.
If the knight’s advantage is reach at the gallop, answer with a longer static reach and cheap training—mass closes the distance economics against horse estates.
Close-order infantry was already normalized; chemical energy removes the decade-per-man skill curve and collapses the nobility monopoly on decisive shock.
Pike-and-shot is a payroll and drill problem, not a seasonal vassal obligation—the social contract that fed knights yields to the contract that feeds volleys.

title: Steam diffusion over seventeen centuries
blurb: From Hero’s spinning toy to Watt’s machines — almost two millennia where the physics of gas and vacuum had to become thinkable, demonstrable, and paid for before “railroad time.”

steps.edge_note: Hero proved sealed vapor can spin; coal is the long fuse—dense fuel stockpiled centuries before anyone earns a living optimizing a cylinder against it.
Pits go where wood no longer reaches; lift limits turn into daily accounts—pressure as stacked geometry in liquids is the vocabulary later borrowed for air.
Once water columns behave predictably, the sloppier lumping of every vapor as generic “air” becomes the next debt—distinct gases make experiments composable.
Classification meets a paying puzzle: lift pumps stalled at ~33 ft, so atmospheric weight stops being philosophy and becomes a number on a ruler.
Torricelli measured the void; Guericke’s seals make it something you can manufacture, break, and repair—repeatable craft instead of one-off glassware luck.
Bench curiosity scales to theater: when teams of horses can’t pull hemispheres apart, sponsors—not just natural philosophers—see that vacuum does macroscopic work.
Public proofs of air’s strength invite the boring next step: squeeze the spring in a controlled way until volume and pressure trade off as a design rule.
Boyle hands designers a compressible rule; Papin bolts it onto Hero’s sealed-kettle intuition—the first sealed steam that earns dinner, not tenure.
Credible small boilers meet the customer who cannot refuse a bad pump—flooded English collieries pay for Savery’s violent shortcut because the fuel base is already coal.
A year later, still burning coal to argue with gravity, Amontons adds temperature to the gas-law family—another scalar for anyone who will soon count duty per bushel.

Amontons finishes the ‘gas plus heat’ picture on the bench; the paying problem is still the flooded seam—Newcomen trades Savery’s high-pressure terror for a slower beat collieries will actually run underground.
Terrible duty per bushel makes “missing” heat in phase changes economically visible—Black gives accountants a place for heat that does not register on a thermometer yet.
Watt’s repair assignment applies that bookkeeping to geometry: always-hot versus always-cold space is how latent heat stops being wasted motion in the cylinder.
Rotary output and steadier pressure fold the toy line into mills—the same fire that once entertained courts now signs factory ledgers.

title: Two centuries between seeing and believing
blurb: From animalcules in ditch water to penicillin by the gram — two centuries where you could watch contagion swim and the hospital still blamed "bad air".

steps.edge_note: Spectacle glass bought a second scale; Harvey’s loop made the body a closed plumbing problem—fevers had to live *somewhere* in the circuit, not in the four humors.
Stacked lenses were a toy until someone aimed them at ditch water: “animalcules” proved life at a scale physicians had no ward vocabulary for.
Smaller still, and named before anyone had a theory of disease—visibility without a job description.
Empiricism runs ahead of theory: deliberate pus from a mild case stops the lethal one—Turkish practice, English controversy, no agreed germ in sight.
Morgagni’s 640 autopsies make death legible organ by organ; the corpse table becomes evidence even while the living patient is still explained by bad air.
Jenner systematizes the trick—cowpox blisters as a manufactured shield—immunity without knowing what you are blocking.
Ether buys painless cutting; operations multiply, and the wound you cannot feel becomes the new killer—surgery’s bottleneck shifts from pain to what walks in on the hands.
Semmelweis counts bodies: the same doctor, different wards—contagion by contact, not miasma, years before anyone agrees on a microbe.
Wine merchants pay for spoilage answers; heating kills what the lens already showed—biology as quality control before biology as bedside doctrine.
The swan-neck flask kills “life from broth” on the bench; the open question moves from creation to *delivery*—germs ride dust, not vapor.
Pasteur gathers the threads: contagious disease has agents; medicine finally has something to hunt besides humors and smells.
Lister weds phenol to Lister’s own problem—clean the cut, not just the air—anesthesia made the OR busy; antisepsis makes it survivable.
Koch grows anthrax outside the body and pins one shape to one plague—identification becomes laboratory craft, not bedside argument.
Jenner’s one-off becomes a recipe: attenuate in the lab when nature offers no mild cousin—manufactured weakness as armor.
The same factory ships a bite protocol across species lines—rabies, not smallpox, is the public proof that the pipeline generalizes.
Fleming’s contaminated dish is a bench accident; the mold’s halo says some cells are killable without poisoning the patient—if anyone can purify it.
Florey and Chain turn halo into grams; WWII demand finishes what germ theory started—mass death finally pays for mass production of cure.
